subject: Creativity
title: Wicked Problems: When Design Thinking Meets Chaos
description: Learn Wicked Problems: When Design Thinking Meets Chaos in one minute.

hook.text: How do you solve poverty? Climate change? Healthcare inequality?

buildup.text: Horst Rittel coined 'wicked problems' in 1973 — problems with no clear definition, no stopping rule, and no right.

discovery.text: Each attempt to solve a wicked problem changes the problem itself.

twist.text: Traditional engineering approaches fail on wicked problems. They need design thinking's iterative, empathetic.

climax.text: You can't 'solve' wicked problems. You can only improve them — continuously, iteratively, and humbly.

punchline.text: Some problems can't be solved. They can only be managed — wisely and endlessly.

quiz.question: What defines a 'wicked problem'?
options: It has no clear definition, no stopping rule, and changes when addressed

details.summary: Wicked problems are challenges so complex that they resist clear definition, let alone solutions. Climate change, poverty, and healthcare access are wicked because every solution creates new problems. Design thinking approaches wicked problems through continuous iteration rather than final answers.
details.whyItMatters: Most of society's most important challenges are wicked problems. Understanding their nature prevents the frustration of expecting neat solutions and enables productive engagement with irreducible complexity.
takeaways: Wicked problems resist complete definition and final solutions
Every intervention in a wicked problem changes the problem itself
Iterative approaches work better than comprehensive master plans

faq.question: What makes a problem wicked?
faq.answer: A wicked problem has no definitive formulation, no stopping rule, and no right or wrong solutions, only better or worse ones. Stakeholders disagree on the problem definition itself. Every solution attempt permanently changes the problem landscape.

faq.question: Can wicked problems ever be solved?
faq.answer: Not in the traditional sense of solved and finished. They can be managed, improved, and addressed through continuous adaptive action. The goal shifts from finding the solution to continuous improvement through iteration, experimentation, and learning.
